text: Within Bangladeshi communities in the UK and within families, Bangladeshi individuals actively engage in teaching and sharing their language, history, and traditions with their spouses, children, friends, and in-laws. The goal of this behavior is to preserve and pass down their rich cultural heritage to the next generation. Recipients, including spouses, children, and friends, are encouraged to learn and actively engage with this cultural knowledge. Additionally, it is noted that in-laws may also express interest in learning about the Bangladeshi cultural roots. This practice is widely regarded as a common and normative behavior within the sampled population, reflecting the community's commitment to preserving their cultural identity and heritage.

Within the multicultural society and Bangladeshi community, Bangladeshi people, particularly the younger generation, actively strive to assimilate into American culture while preserving their cultural uniqueness and promoting openness. Their goal is to be perceived as American while maintaining their cultural identity and fostering unity. This behavior emphasizes the importance of acknowledging and preserving religious and cultural differences while aiming for assimilation and unity. The sampled population reflects a moderate level of normativity regarding this behavior, indicating that a significant portion of the population agrees with this approach, but it is not universally embraced. This reflects the complex dynamics of assimilation, cultural preservation, and unity within the Bangladeshi community and the broader multicultural society.

In Bangladesh, interactions between Bangladeshi people and tourists often involve navigating cultural norms and differences. Bangladeshi individuals may engage in behaviors that are considered acceptable within their culture but may be perceived as nonsensical or rude by foreigners, such as carrying out certain acts and wearing bikinis in public. Their goal is to preserve and express their cultural identity, leading to frustration when faced with perceived rudeness or insensitivity. Conversely, foreigners may unintentionally engage in behaviors perceived as culturally insensitive, prompting responses from Bangladeshi individuals that range from jokes to frustration. These interactions are influenced by differences in cultural norms, etiquette, and religious sensitivity. The behavior is considered controversial among the sampled population, reflecting the challenges and misunderstandings that can arise from cultural differences.

In Bangladesh, when interacting with foreigners, both locals and foreigners engage in behaviors such as expressing pride, offering help, and reacting to unfamiliar actions. These reactions may include staring, waiting, and honking. The goal behind these behaviors is to express pride in their culture, offer assistance, or respond to unfamiliar customs. When interacting with each other, both parties exhibit similar expressions of pride or reactions to unfamiliar behaviors. This cultural norm is widely regarded as common among the sampled population, indicating that these behaviors are considered standard and expected in interactions between Bangladeshi people and foreigners.

Communication style with Bengali people usually depends on the degree of acquaintance. For a close relative or friend, you usually speak directly. For a distant acquaintance or a professional contact, it is more customary to speak indirectly. People generally avoid confrontation and being rude to one another, so speaking indirectly helps facilitate this. When communicating it’s often the case that people will tell you what you want to hear in order to be polite. It’s best to be patient and see what non-verbal actions follow the communication. One Bengali proverb to be aware of is "face is the index of mind". Most people show strong deference to elders and women.

An arm’s length or more of personal space is usually the norm for any formal/business communication. For members of the same sex, holding hands, touching the arm, or putting hands around shoulders is acceptable, except in formal situations or with strangers. For opposite sexes, it is not acceptable to touch. Younger generations nowadays tend to be more western in their approach.

Time tends to be very casually viewed and maintained in most areas of the country. It is customary to be late to start meetings or social events, so many people often show up late. This is true both for personal and professional pursuits. Private bus services nowadays mostly run on time. The government train service is not too bad in being punctual, except when there are accidents or other “unavoidable delays”, which are pretty common. People give time freely, except when they are trying to avoid you. In a social setting, friends may arrive more than two hours late

Depending on the area, women's rights are either somewhat established, dawning, or basically non-existent. In most rural areas, women are seen as caregivers, mothers, and not much more. While opportunities for women in urban areas are increasing, there is still a great disparity with men. Women work, so a family that is middle class or above will hire help to raise children. The thumbs up sign is considered a rude gesture. It is common to remove one's shoes at places of worship, when visiting people's homes, and even in certain shops and businesses. A good rule to follow is if you see shoes arranged near the door, take yours as well. The head wobble, which is common, can mean "yes" and not "no". It depends on the angle and expression and the speed to determine which is which. To beckon someone, you hold your hand palm out, fingers up, and move the fingers towards the palm. You would point subtly, like with an open palm or several fingers. The middle finger is still considered obscene. Kissing or hugging in public is a major taboo. Smoking or talking loudly in front of elders is considered rude. In general loud behavior , including any expression of anger is to be avoided. Drinking is illegal and punishable by prison sentence, except for licensed drinkers and distributors. However, because the laws are generally not well enforced, many people do drink covertly. The legal smoking age is 15 but it is not readily enforced. Many kids at grades 6-7 smoke. Penalties for possession, use, or trafficking in illegal drugs in are severe, and convicted offenders can expect long jail sentences and heavy fines. Drugs are more available than alcohol. Use of all substances is punishable with jail time/fines, as the country is governed by Sharia law, but avoidable with a substantial bribe. Smoking cigarettes is permissible although not common.

Dress is quite conservative for both men and women. For Men : conservative, dark colored suits. Wear shoes that are easy to slip on and off if possible. For Women : conservative business suits or dresses and blouses are appropriate. Avoid tight fitting and revealing clothing, as well sleeveless attire. Dresses should not reveal too much of the legs. Jeans and less casual attire are not recommended for a first meeting.

Titles are important and it is best to address people directly by using their professional title or Mr., Mrs., or Miss, followed by the surname. Many people refer to one another using the surname followed by the suffix “ji”. This is used as a sign of respect. It's best to wait to be invited before using someone's first name. Business cards are usually handed out after the initial handshake and/or greeting. Always present and receive business cards with your right hand. It is best to treat business cards with respect so avoid folding or writing on them.

Arrive at meetings on time even though you may be kept waiting. Meetings usually begin with a fair amount of small-talk and often times no business is discussed during the initial meeting. Meeting agendas and schedules tend to be loosely followed and it is common for meetings to run lengthy. As Bangladesh is a very hierarchical society it is usually best to defer to the most senior person in the room when it comes to beginning and guiding conversations . Periods of silence are considered acceptable and are to be expected. Avoid interrupting and talking over someone if possible. As most Bengali value an indirect communication style, it is likely they will avoid using no in answering questions. They tend to say, “maybe”, or “that would be difficult”.

Avoid hard selling, pressure tactics and any sort of conflict or confrontation. Saving face and maintaining the semblance of harmony is important. D ecisions usually come from the top down and tend to take some time to be made.

Gifts are not usually exchanged at a first business meeting. If invited to a Bengali home, it is appropriate to bring chocolates, pastries or sweets. Avoid bringing wine or any liquor. Gifts are not to be opened when they are received. It is best to do this in private. It is best to give and receive gifts with the both hands.

Dress is conservative — men wear pants, younger men may wear shorts, and both may wear traditional dress at special events. Women usually wear the traditional dress to avoid attracting stares. Classes are in both lecture and discussion format, and somewhat creative.

For dating, men usually ask out women but are not very forward. Holding hands can provoke criticism, and PDA is unacceptable. Smoking cigarettes is permissible although not common. There are underground clubs for the wealthy, where alcohol is available. At universities there are dry parties.
